presentingComplaint: Rapid onset of a hot, swollen, exquisitely painful right knee with fever for 2 days.
history: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with a 2-day history of severe right knee pain that began abruptly, associated with swelling, warmth, and inability to bear weight. He reports fever with chills starting the same day as the joint pain. No preceding trauma. No history of similar episodes, gout, or pseudogout. No recent joint injection. He denies IV drug use. He has a history of a minor abrasion on the ipsilateral shin 5 days ago that has since become mildly erythematous. No urethral discharge, diarrhea, or preceding conjunctivitis to suggest reactive arthritis. No other joints involved.
examination: Toxic-appearing, uncomfortable man lying still with the right knee held in slight flexion. Right knee is markedly swollen, erythematous, and warm with a large effusion; skin over the joint is tense and shiny. Severe pain on any attempted active or passive range of motion (guarding), with pain out of proportion to gentle palpation. No crepitus or bullae. No overlying skin breakdown or draining sinus. Small area of cellulitic erythema over the ipsilateral shin abrasion, non-fluctuant, without ascending lymphangitic streaking. No other joints swollen or tender. No cardiac murmur. No skin pustules, tenosynovitis, or rash to suggest disseminated gonococcal infection.
imaging: Plain radiograph right knee: joint effusion, soft tissue swelling, no bony erosion or osteomyelitis at presentation
Point-of-care/formal ultrasound right knee: confirms large effusion, guides diagnostic aspiration
microbiology: Synovial fluid Gram stain: Gram-positive cocci in clusters
Synovial fluid culture: pending (subsequently grew Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin-susceptible, in this scenario)
Blood cultures: sent x2 sets before antibiotics, pending
finalDiagnosis: Septic arthritis (bacterial, non-gonococcal) of the right knee, likely Staphylococcus aureus
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Infectious Arthritis
IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines - Native Joint Septic Arthritis (relevant general IDSA framework)
stewardship: Empirical IV antibiotics targeting Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA coverage pending local resistance data and risk factors) and streptococci should be started promptly after synovial fluid and blood cultures are obtained, with urgent orthopedic consultation for joint drainage (arthrocentesis/arthroscopic washout); narrow therapy once organism and susceptibilities are known.
contraindications: Do not delay empirical antibiotics or source control awaiting culture results in a toxic-appearing patient
Avoid intra-articular corticosteroid injection until septic arthritis is excluded
Avoid NSAID/analgesic masking of exam findings before diagnostic aspiration is performed
edgeCases: Diabetes mellitus increases risk of S. aureus septic arthritis and worse outcomes
Concurrent skin/soft tissue infection (shin abrasion with cellulitis) may be the bacteremic source

Gonococcal arthritis is an important differential in sexually active adults and can present with migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, and pustular rash (dermatitis-arthritis syndrome) - absent here
